summary.text: The estimate \(C_{n+1}\ge (5/2)C_n\) for \(n\ge2\) bounds reciprocal tails by a geometric series, making the reciprocal at the first index where two intervals differ larger than all later discrepancies. Every nonexceptional admissible sum lies strictly between \(0\) and \(1\), while the sole exceptional sum equals \(1\), so taking fractional parts preserves the separation.

full_proof.text:
Let
\[
C_n=\frac1{n+1}\binom{2n}{n}\qquad(n\ge 0)
\]
be the Catalan numbers, and for integers \(1\le j\le k\) put
\[
S(j,k)=\sum_{i=j}^k\frac1{C_i}.
\]
We prove that, among the pairs satisfying
\[
0<\min\{2,k\}\le j\le k,
\]
the numbers \(S(j,k)\) have pairwise distinct fractional parts.

The proof rests on the fact that, beginning at \(C_2\), every reciprocal Catalan number is larger than the sum of any finite collection of all the later reciprocal Catalan numbers.

### 1. A growth estimate for the Catalan numbers

The Catalan formula gives the standard recurrence
\[
(n+2)C_{n+1}=2(2n+1)C_n. \tag{1}
\]
Indeed,
\[
\frac{C_{n+1}}{C_n}
 =\frac{\binom{2n+2}{n+1}/(n+2)}{\binom{2n}{n}/(n+1)}
 =\frac{(2n+2)(2n+1)}{(n+1)^2}\frac{n+1}{n+2}
 =\frac{2(2n+1)}{n+2}.
\]
All Catalan numbers are positive. If \(n\ge2\), then
\[
5(n+2)\le4(2n+1),
\]
because this inequality is equivalent to \(6\le3n\). Multiplying by the positive number \(C_n\) and using (1), we obtain
\[
5C_n\le 2C_{n+1}\qquad(n\ge2). \tag{2}
\]
Equivalently,
\[
\frac1{C_{n+1}}\le \frac25\frac1{C_n}\qquad(n\ge2). \tag{3}
\]
Iterating (2), for every \(m\ge2\) and every integer \(r\ge0\), gives
\[
5^rC_m\le2^rC_{m+r}.
\]
After division by the positive quantity \(5^rC_mC_{m+r}\), this becomes
\[
\frac1{C_{m+r}}\le \left(\frac25\right)^r\frac1{C_m}. \tag{4}
\]

We now deduce the required tail estimate. For every \(m\ge2\) and every \(k\),
\[
\sum_{i=m+1}^k\frac1{C_i}<\frac1{C_m}, \tag{5}
\]
where the sum is understood to be zero if \(k<m+1\). The empty case is immediate. Otherwise write \(N=k-m\ge1\). By (4),
\[
\sum_{i=m+1}^k\frac1{C_i}
 =\sum_{r=1}^{N}\frac1{C_{m+r}}
 \le \frac1{C_m}\sum_{r=1}^{N}\left(\frac25\right)^r.
\]
The finite geometric sum is
\[
\sum_{r=1}^{N}\left(\frac25\right)^r
 =\frac23\left(1-\left(\frac25\right)^N\right)
 <\frac23<1.
\]
This proves (5). Thus a reciprocal Catalan term with index at least \(2\) strictly dominates every finite tail following it.

### 2. Distinct finite intervals beginning at index at least 2 have distinct sums

We prove a slightly more structural statement. Let
\[
I_1=\{j_1,j_1+1,\dots,k_1\},\qquad
I_2=\{j_2,j_2+1,\dots,k_2\},
\]
where \(2\le j_r\le k_r\), and suppose \(I_1\ne I_2\). Then
\[
\sum_{i\in I_1}\frac1{C_i}\ne
\sum_{i\in I_2}\frac1{C_i}. \tag{6}
\]

Suppose to the contrary that the two sums are equal. Decompose each interval into its intersection with the other and its difference from the other:
\[
\sum_{i\in I_1\setminus I_2}\frac1{C_i}
 +\sum_{i\in I_1\cap I_2}\frac1{C_i}
 =
\sum_{i\in I_2\setminus I_1}\frac1{C_i}
 +\sum_{i\in I_1\cap I_2}\frac1{C_i}.
\]
Cancelling the common intersection yields
\[
\sum_{i\in I_1\setminus I_2}\frac1{C_i}
 =
\sum_{i\in I_2\setminus I_1}\frac1{C_i}. \tag{7}
\]
Both set differences must be nonempty. For if, say, \(I_1\setminus I_2\) were empty, then the left side of (7) would be zero. Since every \(1/C_i\) is positive, the right side could be zero only if \(I_2\setminus I_1\) were also empty. The two intervals would then be equal, contrary to the hypothesis. The same argument applies with the roles reversed.

Let \(m\) be the least element of the symmetric difference
\[
(I_1\setminus I_2)\cup(I_2\setminus I_1).
\]
Because both intervals begin at indices at least \(2\), we have \(m\ge2\). There are two cases.

First suppose \(m\in I_1\setminus I_2\). Every element of \(I_2\setminus I_1\) is then strictly greater than \(m\): it cannot be less than \(m\), by the minimality of \(m\), and it cannot equal \(m\), because \(m\in I_1\) whereas every element of \(I_2\setminus I_1\) is outside \(I_1\). Also, every such element is at most \(k_2\). Therefore positivity of the terms and the tail estimate (5) give
\[
\sum_{i\in I_2\setminus I_1}\frac1{C_i}
 \le \sum_{i=m+1}^{k_2}\frac1{C_i}
 <\frac1{C_m}.
\]
On the other hand, \(m\in I_1\setminus I_2\), so
\[
\sum_{i\in I_1\setminus I_2}\frac1{C_i}\ge\frac1{C_m}.
\]
These inequalities contradict (7).

If instead \(m\in I_2\setminus I_1\), the same argument with \(I_1\) and \(I_2\) interchanged gives
\[
\sum_{i\in I_1\setminus I_2}\frac1{C_i}<\frac1{C_m}
\le\sum_{i\in I_2\setminus I_1}\frac1{C_i},
\]
again contradicting (7). This proves (6).

We will also use the elementary fact that a nonempty integer interval determines its endpoints. Explicitly, if
\[
\{j_1,j_1+1,\dots,k_1\}=\{j_2,j_2+1,\dots,k_2\}
\]
and \(j_r\le k_r\), then the least elements are equal, so \(j_1=j_2\), and the greatest elements are equal, so \(k_1=k_2\). Consequently, distinct endpoint pairs satisfying \(j_r\le k_r\) give distinct interval sets.

### 3. The size and fractional part of every nonexceptional admissible sum

Consider an admissible pair \((j,k)\), so
\[
0<\min\{2,k\}\le j\le k. \tag{8}
\]
Since \(\min\{2,k\}>0\), necessarily \(k\ge1\). If \(k=1\), then \(\min\{2,k\}=1\), and (8) forces \(j=1\). Thus the only admissible pair with \(k<2\) is
\[
(j,k)=(1,1). \tag{9}
\]
Every other admissible pair has \(k\ge2\), and then \(\min\{2,k\}=2\), so
\[
2\le j\le k. \tag{10}
\]

For a pair satisfying (10), the sum \(S(j,k)\) is positive because it is a nonempty sum of positive terms. It is also less than \(1\). Indeed,
\[
S(j,k)\le\sum_{i=2}^k\frac1{C_i}
 =\frac1{C_2}+\sum_{i=3}^k\frac1{C_i}.
\]
Now \(C_2=2\), and (5), applied with \(m=2\), says
\[
\sum_{i=3}^k\frac1{C_i}<\frac1{C_2}=\frac12.
\]
Hence
\[
0<S(j,k)<\frac12+\frac12=1. \tag{11}
\]
A real number in \([0,1)\) is its own fractional part. Therefore, for every admissible pair other than \((1,1)\),
\[
\{S(j,k)\}=S(j,k), \tag{12}
\]
where \(\{x\}=x-\lfloor x\rfloor\) denotes the fractional part.

For the exceptional pair, \(C_1=1\), and hence
\[
S(1,1)=\frac1{C_1}=1,
\qquad
\{S(1,1)\}=0. \tag{13}
\]
By (11), the fractional part belonging to every other admissible pair is strictly positive. Thus the exceptional pair's fractional part is distinct from all the others.

### 4. Completion of the pairwise-distinctness argument

Take two distinct admissible endpoint pairs \((j_1,k_1)\ne(j_2,k_2)\).

If one of them is \((1,1)\), then its fractional part is \(0\) by (13). The other pair is nonexceptional, so its fractional part equals its sum and is strictly positive by (11) and (12). Their fractional parts are therefore distinct.

It remains to consider the case in which neither pair is \((1,1)\). Then (10) gives
\[
2\le j_1\le k_1,
\qquad
2\le j_2\le k_2.
\]
Since the endpoint pairs are distinct and each interval is nonempty, their integer interval sets are distinct. Statement (6) therefore gives
\[
S(j_1,k_1)\ne S(j_2,k_2).
\]
Both sums lie strictly between \(0\) and \(1\), so each is equal to its own fractional part. Their fractional parts are consequently distinct.

This covers every possible pair of admissible intervals and proves the conjecture.
